Complete Empirical Research Plan  

────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy  
Instrumental-Variables (two-stage least squares).  
Quarter-of-birth generates exogenous variation in years of completed schooling because compulsory‐attendance laws bind at a birthday, while school entry is by calendar year. Quarter of birth is therefore a powerful, plausibly exogenous instrument for schooling. IV is preferred to OLS because it corrects both (a) ability-bias and family-background confounding and (b) measurement error in reported schooling.

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
• Sᵢ = Years of completed schooling (continuous).  

Instrument (“treatment assignment”)  
• Zᵢ = 1[born in first calendar quarter] or a set of three dummies Q1, Q2, Q3 with Q4 omitted.  
(Results are almost identical whether the instrument is Q1 alone or the full set.)

Control group  
• Workers born in later quarters provide the counterfactual schooling and earnings distribution for those born in the first quarter.

Timing  
• The “assignment” (birth quarter) is fixed at conception; there is no staggered timing after birth, so a standard cross-section IV suffices.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1 Relevance Quarter of birth must predict completed schooling.  
 Plausibility: Institutional logic plus prior tabulations show Q1 births average ≈0.15 fewer years of schooling than Q4 births; first-stage F-stat ≫ 10.

A2 Exclusion Restriction Conditional on cohort, state of birth, race and other observables, quarter of birth affects earnings only through schooling.  
 Plausibility: Conception timing is unlikely to be correlated with innate ability or parental human capital within state-year cells; still needs scrutiny (see threats).

A3 Independence Quarter of birth is as good as randomly assigned within cohort-state cells.  
 Plausibility: Parents rarely choose conception month based on expected child earnings 20–50 years hence.

A4 Monotonicity (LATE) Being born earlier in the calendar year never increases schooling for anyone (no “defiers”).  
 Plausibility: Legal dropout age structure ensures later entry cannot shorten compulsory attendance.

A5 Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) One individual’s quarter of birth does not change another’s schooling/earnings.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable in this context.

4. Main Threats & Mitigations  

T1 Season-of-birth effects unrelated to schooling  
 • Could reflect prenatal health, parental SES seasonality, farm labor demand, etc.  
 Mitigation:  
  – Include rich controls: year-of-birth FE, state-of-birth FE, race dummies.  
  – Show that quarter of birth does NOT predict mother’s education or family income in Census samples with parental info (placebo test).  
  – Estimate reduced-form on outcomes measured before substantial labor-market exposure (e.g., probability of military service) to confirm no direct effect.

T2 Differential mortality or migration by quarter  
 • If low-SES Q1 babies are less likely to survive to adulthood, estimates may be biased.  
 Mitigation: Compare infant-mortality and migration rates by quarter using Vital Statistics; limit sample to birth-state residents; re-weight for survival if needed.

T3 State-specific compulsory-school-age law differences over time  
 • Heterogeneity in d(AgeLaw − EntryAge) across states may dilute or confound first stage.  
 Mitigation:  
  – Interact quarter dummies with state-specific compulsory-age indicators.  
  – Use just‐identified specification with Q1×StateAgeLaw as instrument.  
  – Cluster standard errors at state-of-birth level.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
###########################################
# 0. Packages
###########################################
library(data.table)  # fast loading
library(fixest)      # fast IV and FE estimators
library(modelsummary)
library(AER)         # ivreg for robustness

###########################################
# 1. Load & merge data
###########################################
c70 <- fread("census70_pums.csv")
c80 <- fread("census80_pums.csv")
census <- rbindlist(list(c70, c80), fill = TRUE)

###########################################
# 2. Variable construction
###########################################
census[, yob  := as.integer(year_of_birth)]
census[, qob  := quarter(birth_month)]           # 1,2,3,4
census[, q1   := as.integer(qob == 1)]
census[, q2   := as.integer(qob == 2)]
census[, q3   := as.integer(qob == 3)]           # q4 is omitted
census[, educ := years_schooling]                # assume raw variable
census[, lnw  := log(annual_earnings)]           # winsorize later if desired

###########################################
# 3. Sample restrictions
###########################################
census <- census[sex == "Male" &
                 race %in% c("White","Black") &
                 yob %between% c(1930,1959) &
                 lnw > 0]                        # exclude zero earnings

###########################################
# 4. Main two-stage least squares
###########################################
iv_main <- feols(lnw ~ 1 | educ ~ q1 + q2 + q3,            # 2SLS formula
                 data = census,
                 feprefix = "fe",
                 cluster = ~state_birth + yob)             # two-way clustering

summary(iv_main)

###########################################
# 5. Robustness: include state×cohort FE
###########################################
census[, state_by_yob := interaction(state_birth, yob)]

iv_robust <- feols(lnw ~ 1 | educ ~ q1 + q2 + q3,
                   data = census,
                   fe = ~state_by_yob + race,
                   cluster = ~state_birth)

etable(list("Main" = iv_main, "State×Cohort FE" = iv_robust),
       se = "cluster")

###########################################
# 6. Placebo test: outcome = adult height
###########################################
placebo <- feols(height_inches ~ 1 | educ ~ q1 + q2 + q3,
                 data = census,
                 fe = ~state_by_yob + race,
                 cluster = ~state_birth)
summary(placebo)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic theory (human-capital model) and prior empirical work suggest a positive effect. Mincerian OLS returns are roughly 10 % per year; IV studies usually find slightly higher returns when measurement error dominates ability bias or slightly lower when ability bias dominates. Prior: one extra year of schooling raises annual earnings by ≈8 % (β ≈ 0.08 in logs).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  
C1 Instrument relevance………………1  
C2 Exclusion restriction………………0.7 (plausible but testable threats)  
C3 Random assignment of Z…………1  
C4 Monotonicity…………………………1  
C5 No interference (SUTVA)…………1  

Total ≈ 4.7 / 5 → high internal validity, subject mainly to verifying no direct quarter-of-birth effects.
